w: Building began around 1210 under bishops Jocelin of Wells and Reginald Fitz Jocelin. Bishop Ralph of Shrewsbury added the walls, gatehouse and moat in the 14th century, diverting streams to fill it. The great hall was partly demolished around 1830, but the current bishop still lives in part of the palace.
s: A moated palace still home to the bishop
_facts: Building started c.1210 by bishops Jocelin of Wells and Reginald Fitz Jocelin
Walls, gatehouse and moat added 14th century by Bishop Ralph of Shrewsbury
Great hall partly demolished c.1830
Still partly a residence for the current bishop

w: The earliest recorded church here dates to a charter of 766; a bishopric followed in 909, only for the cathedral to relocate to Bath Abbey in 1090. Wells regained co-cathedral status in 1218. The cruciform cathedral rose in two campaigns: an Early English nave from around 1180, a Decorated Gothic east end from 1285.
s: Cruciform, Gothic, and a cathedral since 766
_facts: Earliest recorded church on site: charter of 766
Cathedral moved to Bath Abbey in 1090, Wells regained co-cathedral status 1218
Built in two campaigns, c.1180-1260 and c.1285-1345
Over 300,000 visitors a year (2023)

w: Cave hyenas denned here before people did; humans and Neanderthals then used the caves on and off for some 45,000 years, leaving Palaeolithic tools and butchered bones. A corn mill worked the River Axe here since the 1086 Domesday survey, and Britain's oldest working paper mill has run since about 1610.
s: Hyena dens, Neanderthals, and cheese-maturing caves
_facts: Used by cave hyenas, then humans and Neanderthals over ~45,000 years
Corn mill recorded on the site since the 1086 Domesday survey
Oldest working paper mill in Britain, running since c.1610
Constant 11C used for maturing Cheddar cheese

w: Often mistaken for the cathedral it stands near, St Cuthbert's is in fact the parish church, dating from the 13th century. It carries a fine Somerset stone tower and a carved roof rated among the best of its kind, and is Grade I listed in its own right.
s: Mistaken for the cathedral, but its own parish church
_facts: Parish church dating from the 13th century
Often mistaken for Wells Cathedral
Fine Somerset stone tower and carved roof
Grade I listed

w: Reportedly Europe's oldest residential street with its original buildings intact -- John Julius Norwich called it 'that rarest of survivals, a planned street of the mid-14th century.' Bishop Ralph of Shrewsbury built it for the Vicars Choral; the hall was finished in 1348.
s: Europe's oldest planned street, built for the choir
_facts: Reportedly Europe's oldest residential street with original buildings intact
Built for the Vicars Choral by Bishop Ralph of Shrewsbury
Vicars' Hall completed 1348, houses built into the 1420s
Tapered width creates a forced-perspective illusion of length

w: At 305 metres, the second-highest point on the Mendip Hills, crowned by a 281-metre TV mast and, far older, a Neolithic long barrow. On a clear day the view runs south to Wells Cathedral two miles off and on to the Blackdown and Quantock hills beyond.
s: Mendip views to Wells Cathedral, two miles off
_facts: 305-metre summit, second-highest point on the Mendip Hills
Mendip TV Mast, 281 metres high, on the hill
Neolithic long barrow, a Scheduled Ancient Monument
Views to Wells Cathedral, and to distant Somerset hills
